source_results.title: Triboluminescence Definition and Examples - Cold Light

concepts.mechanism_summary: Triboluminescence is the emission of light when a material is mechanically pulled apart, ripped, scratched, crushed, or rubbed. The phenomenon appears in most cases to be caused by the separation and reunification of static electric charges; when the charges recombine, the electric discharge ionizes the surrounding air, causing a flash of light. Crystals displaying triboluminescence must lack symmetry to permit charge separation and be poor conductors.

atoms.verbatim_quote: upon fracture of asymmetrical materials, charge is separated. When the charges recombine, the electrical discharge ionizes the surrounding air, causing a flash of light. The charge separation leads to a potential difference of about 40,000 Volts
atoms.mechanism_atom: Mechanical fracture of asymmetric crystal induces charge separation (~40 kV) which upon recombination produces ionizing electric discharge and light emission

atoms.verbatim_quote: Cleavage, peeling, grinding, crushing, and many other processes can also lead to discharge at interface, thus converting mechanical energy into light energy
atoms.mechanism_atom: Interfacial mechanical stress transforms kinetic/strain energy into photonic emission via electric discharge at fracture surfaces

atoms.verbatim_quote: Triboluminescent materials are widely used in the construction industry for crack detection as well as damage assessment using image processing and machine learning protocols
atoms.mechanism_atom: Crack-tip stress field activates mechanoluminescent emission which is then classified by GAN+CNN dual machine learning for structural health monitoring

source_results.title: Sonoluminescence as a Physical Vacuum Excitation

concepts.mechanism_summary: Sonoluminescence occurs when a sound wave of sufficient intensity induces a gaseous cavity within a liquid to collapse quickly, emitting a burst of light; the temperature inside the bubble can reach up to 12,000–20,000 kelvins. The exact mechanism remains unknown; competing theories include hotspot thermal emission, bremsstrahlung, and collision-induced radiation. One hypothesis (Eberlein) proposes the rapidly moving bubble interface converts virtual photons into real photons via a process similar to Hawking radiation.

atoms.verbatim_quote: a sound wave of sufficient intensity induces a gaseous cavity within a liquid to collapse quickly, emitting a burst of light. The temperature inside the bubble during single-bubble sonoluminescence could reach up to 12,000 kelvins

source_results.title: Spinodal Decomposition - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics

concepts.mechanism_summary: Spinodal decomposition is a mechanism by which a single thermodynamic phase spontaneously separates into two phases without nucleation, occurring when the second derivative of the Gibbs free energy with respect to composition is negative (negative curvature), making the system unstable to infinitesimal fluctuations. A fast quench moves the system into the unstable spinodal region, enabling 'uphill' diffusion that amplifies initial composition fluctuations. The dynamics are commonly modeled by the Cahn-Hilliard equation.

atoms.verbatim_quote: Spinodal decomposition is a mechanism by which a single thermodynamic phase spontaneously separates into two phases (without nucleation). Decomposition occurs when there is no thermodynamic barrier to phase separation
atoms.mechanism_atom: Negative free-energy curvature separates a homogeneous phase into two co-existing phases spontaneously without nucleation barrier

atoms.verbatim_quote: the thermodynamic driving force for spinodal decomposition arises in regions of the phase diagram where the second derivative of the Gibbs free energy of mixing with respect to composition is negative (∂²ΔG/∂x² < 0), rendering the system unstable to small perturbations and enabling 'uphill' diffusion that amplifies initial fluctuations
atoms.mechanism_atom: Uphill diffusion accumulates compositional fluctuations into macroscopic phase-separated domains when free-energy curvature is negative

atoms.verbatim_quote: A Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) can be used to reproduce the time-dependent solutions of the Cahn-Hilliard equation, which describes the spinodal decomposition, focusing on their longtime behavior
atoms.mechanism_atom: Cahn-Hilliard free energy functional regulates the phase-field evolution dynamics that neural networks are trained to emulate

source_results.title: Marangoni Effect - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics

concepts.mechanism_summary: The Marangoni effect (Gibbs-Marangoni effect) is the mass transfer along an interface between two phases due to a gradient of surface tension. Since a liquid with high surface tension pulls more strongly on surrounding liquid than one with low surface tension, a gradient in surface tension causes liquid to flow away from regions of low surface tension. This gradient arises from variations in temperature, solute concentration, or surfactant concentration along the interface.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the presence of a gradient in surface tension will naturally cause the liquid to flow away from regions of low surface tension
atoms.mechanism_atom: A surface tension gradient along a fluid interface induces directed mass flow away from low-surface-tension regions

atoms.verbatim_quote: thermocapillary forces present due to the gradient of surface tension cause the fluid to move toward the surface with increased velocity, which increases the rate of Marangoni convection
atoms.mechanism_atom: Temperature- or concentration-driven surface tension gradients regulate convective flow velocity and direction at fluid interfaces

atoms.verbatim_quote: solutal Marangoni number is the ratio of surface tension induced by a concentration gradient to adhesive force, providing a key parameter for characterizing concentration-driven effects
atoms.mechanism_atom: Differential solute concentration exchanges drive interfacial flow proportional to the solutal Marangoni number

concepts.mechanism_summary: Cavitation occurs when the static pressure of a liquid falls below its vapor pressure, forming small vapor-filled cavities. When these cavities move to higher-pressure regions, the surrounding liquid implodes inward; as the bubble collapses, inward momentum causes a sharp increase in pressure and temperature of the vapor within, generating shock waves that can damage machinery. Cavitation commonly occurs in centrifugal pumps, water turbines, and marine propellers.

atoms.verbatim_quote: when the bubble finally collapses, the inward momentum of the surrounding liquid causes a sharp increase of pressure and temperature of the vapor within. These cavities can generate shock waves that may damage machinery
atoms.mechanism_atom: Bubble collapse produces inward momentum-driven pressure/temperature spike generating erosive shock waves

atoms.verbatim_quote: Cavitation occurs when bubbles are created when pressure drops below saturated vapor pressure, and these cavitation-induced bubbles are unstable in nature—as soon as pressure is reinstated above vapor pressure, bubbles immediately collapse
atoms.mechanism_atom: Sub-vapor-pressure conditions accumulate bubble nucleation events that collapse violently upon pressure restoration

source_results.title: Widmanstätten pattern | Meteorite, Iron-Nickel & Octahedrite | Britannica

concepts.mechanism_summary: The Widmanstätten pattern forms in iron-nickel meteorites through diffusion-controlled solid-state precipitation during extremely slow cooling (100–10,000 °C per million years) between 700 °C and 450 °C. Nickel atoms diffuse out of growing kamacite lamellae into surrounding taenite while iron atoms diffuse oppositely, and the lamellae grow along specific {111} crystallographic planes in the parent taenite to minimize interfacial energy, producing the characteristic cross-hatched intergrowth.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the taenite-to-kamacite transformation is diffusion-controlled in the solid state (700°C to 450°C), with Ni atoms diffusing out of growing kamacite into surrounding taenite while Fe atoms diffuse oppositely
atoms.mechanism_atom: Counter-diffusion of Ni and Fe atoms in solid state separates parent taenite into kamacite and taenite lamellae

atoms.verbatim_quote: kamacite forming along specific {111} crystallographic planes in the parent taenite. The growth of these phases along preferred crystallographic planes minimizes interfacial energy, leading to the characteristic lamellar morphology
atoms.mechanism_atom: Crystallographic preference propagates lamellar growth along {111} planes minimizing interfacial energy

atoms.verbatim_quote: Slow cooling provides time for atomic migration over micrometers to millimeters, allowing macroscopic crystal growth. The formation of nickel-poor kamacite proceeds by diffusion of nickel in the solid alloy at temperatures between 450 and 700 °C, and can only take place during very slow cooling, about 100 to 10,000 °C per million years
atoms.mechanism_atom: Cooling rate regulates the diffusion timescale and hence the spatial scale of phase separation lamellae
